state.brief: Evaluate removing lowercase then from canlang scenarios. This AI-authored CRUD business-SaaS DSL prioritizes adoption, compact tokens, dependable generation and simple canonical primitives. The user raises the removal as a design possibility; that preference is not evidence of safety. No compiler/runtime or generation/token benchmark exists. This question concerns only lowercase then, not scenario, uppercase Given/When/Then, indentation width or minimum-line formatting.
state.facts: Current scenarios have typed parameters and by authorization or on trusted-source identity. Preconditions may occur before then. An inline then introduces simple statements separated by semicolons; a standalone then introduces an indented body containing let, require, effects, return, if and for. One-space indentation defines scope. A mutation is one atomic unit independent of this marker: failed require anywhere rejects provisional effects and delivery intents. Read scenarios allow only pure statements and require a result. The corpus has 254 scenarios and 254 then introducers: 154 standalone and 100 inline. There are 34 require statements inside then blocks. Thus then is not a fixed boundary after all validation. Descriptions use #; attached examples have independently authored expectation rows and are test-only.
state.candidate: Proposed canonical grammar: keep scenario headers and make their ordered direct children the executable body. Remove inline then while retaining its statement sequence. Delete a standalone then and move its descendants one indentation level outward, preserving inner if/else and for nesting. examples stays a distinct reserved test-only block attached to the scenario; its rows do not execute as production statements. Preconditions, intermediate checks, effects, returns, names, permissions and transaction semantics must retain their original order and scopes. Do not hoist requires to the beginning or combine assignments. These are migration obligations, not an assumption that every implementation satisfies them.
state.comparison: Keeping then offers a visible body boundary and a dedicated grammar container separating leading guards from subsequent statements and attached tests. It costs a repeated token per scenario, 154 body-container lines and an extra nesting level in those blocks; the guard/body distinction does not mean all guards occur first. Removing then eliminates that container and lets one ordered statement grammar describe leading and intermediate guards alike. Potential costs include changed parser/diagnostic rules, mis-dedenting nested branches, and accidental treatment of examples as executable children if its test-only boundary is not defined correctly. A direct body must discriminate the existing statements and reserved examples explicitly. Actual token savings and AI error rates are unmeasured. Both policies aim to be one canonical syntax; this is not general semicolon packing.

examples.existing:
scenario finish(item:Item) by=members
 require item.status==open
 then
  let selected=item.Part
  require count(selected)>0
  for part in selected limit=100
   require part.ready
   set part {done=true}
  set item {status=done}
 examples item=fixture_item
  item.status -> item.status
  open -> done
examples.proposed:
scenario finish(item:Item) by=members
 require item.status==open
 let selected=item.Part
 require count(selected)>0
 for part in selected limit=100
  require part.ready
  set part {done=true}
 set item {status=done}
 examples item=fixture_item
  item.status -> item.status
  open -> done

state.limits: The snippets illustrate syntax and nesting with schematic typed entities and a fixture; they are not complete runnable applications or compiled equivalence evidence. Account for risks of both alternatives. Return a yes probability, not an explanation invented beyond the supplied facts.

remove_then.instructions: Should canlang remove lowercase then from scenarios and use the specified ordered direct body instead, weighing the repeated syntax against the delimiter, scope and test-boundary risks?
